newsitem.title: USA: P&G says no-coupon experiment in NY worked.
newsitem.headline: P&G says no-coupon experiment in NY worked.

text.p: Procter & Gamble Co said Thursday it would study the results of a year-long experiment eliminating store coupons in upstate New York that triggered a flood of consumer complaints.
The test, which ended Friday, was part of the consumer goods manufacturer's effort to do away with coupons, which it said are expensive to produce and inefficient for consumers.
"We've already reduced our use of coupons over the last four to five years by over 50 percent," said company spokeswoman Linda Ulrey, who termed the experiment "successful."

"Consumers are paying for coupons, for printing, for distributing," she said. "What we were really trying to do here was think of a way to give the shopper more convenience, as well as providing a good product at a good price."

During the experiment, which was launched in February of last year in upstate New York, Procter & Gamble's product sales in the region were "flat", despite the Ohio-based manufacturer's overall five percent sales growth last year to $35.28 billion.
Ulrey insisted the company was not pressured into ending the no-coupon experiment, but it did receive an undetermined number of customer complaints and threats of boycotts on its products.
"On average during the test period, consumers paid the same for P&G products without coupons than they did with coupons and in many cases they paid less," Ulrey maintained.

She also said the company was cooperating with the ongoing investigation by New York's Attorney General Dennis Vacco, who said in a statement that his office was probing "possible market manipulation" by manufacturers that joined Procter & Gamble in eliminating coupons.

Vacco hailed the resumption of coupon distribution in the region by Procter & Gamble and other manufacturers, including The Clorox Co as a "victory for consumers", many of whom "rely on coupons to help make ends meet."

About 325 million coupons worth billions of dollars are distributed annually across the nation, but some consumer goods manufacturers believe they are expensive, wasteful and inconvenient, and complain that most go unused.
